title: Predicting farmers’ crop choice between hybrid and indigenous varieties based on socio-ecological context and perceived crop advantages in Nepal
content:
by Prience Shrestha, Sujata Shrestha, Tulasa Chaudhary, Uma Dhungel, Sanjita Khanal, Kamal Prasad Aryal, Uttam Babu Shrestha

Farmers in Nepal increasingly combine market-sourced improved seed with indigenous seed that is traditionally saved and shared across local communities. This study aims to examine associations between crop choice, household social-ecological characteristics, and farmers’ concurrent perceptions of the comparative advantages of improved and indigenous crops. We analyzed survey data from 118 households in three municipalities of western Nepal using Random Forest Classifier (RFC) and multiclass One-vs-Rest Support Vector Machine (SVM) models. Complete-case screening retained 108 records for the social-ecological analysis, while 117 records were used for the perception analysis. Data were split before the preprocessing pipeline that involved data imputations, standardization, encoding, and component analysis using the data fitted in the training split across the evaluation and testing datasets. Upmost care was taken to avoid cross-contamination of data characteristics across data splits. Analysis using the selected Machine Learning (ML) algorithms resulted to mere 55% (RFC) and 73% (SVM) accuracy for observed association between social-ecological variables and crop-choice, whereas 75% (RFC) and 83% (SVM) accuracy was observed for association between local perception regarding comparative advantage of a given crop variety against another and crop choice. Associations between social-ecological or perception variables with crop choice involving adoption of improved varieties only could not be estimated when administered through both ML algorithms. Hence, the apparently stronger association between the perception variables and crop choice reflects discrimination between the two larger classes rather than demonstrated performance for improved-only cultivation retaining sparse data availability. The results therefore intend exploratory associations within the surveyed households and do not establish prediction, causation, or regional generalizability.
